prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B003 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Having read the full first round, I note that all six of us arrived at the same trio by reasoning about the discovery arc and not by counting opening ranks, and that is the only basis on which I will vote. The achievement is a discernible change in a field: the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, identification of the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) peptide, human physiology of its secretion and action, receptor and tissue biology, and then agonists whose benefit on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes has been shown in large randomized trials by independent groups. Maturity is not in doubt. The three names map to three separable steps (Holst on native physiology in humans, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology, Mojsov on the active peptide and its synthesis), which is what lets the credit be defended as a set. In reply to the chair's first question, I would frame the citation around the physiology and the active form, with the therapies named as the consequence. That framing is the only one under which these three names, and not a drug-development list, follow from the text.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still attribution and not merit or maturity, and nothing in round 1 repaired it. Knudsen's acylated, albumin-binding analogues are what turned the physiology into a medicine, and if the committee's reading of the achievement shifts toward the therapy, her claim becomes at least as strong as Mojsov's, as El Manira says. Mojsov's standing against Habener and other early peptide investigators rests on recalled accounts that none of us can verify from the supplied files. The citation cannot claim a single origin for GLP-1 biology, and I would want the committee record to say that it is making a judgement between discovery and engineering and not reaching it by default. The fact that all six of us placed this first is also a risk if it reflects the public prominence of the drugs more than a settled allocation of credit.

responses.point: Linnarsson would resolve the B003 allocation by the criterion of discovery rather than development, treating Holst and Drucker as the physiological anchors and Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active form as the step that made the pharmacology possible, and says substituting Knudsen would turn the prize into a drug-development award.
responses.response: I agree with the criterion and I think it is the right answer to the chair's question about Knudsen. Where I would add care is the second half of your argument. If the committee relies on Mojsov's step as the justification, it owns the priority question, and a citation that says 'identification of its active form' makes a specific claim that needs to hold up. I would therefore keep the wording to identification and not 'discovery of GLP-1 itself', and I would accept a committee note acknowledging the long-acting analogue programme and the work of Knudsen and her colleagues as the route to the therapy without crediting it as a fourth name. I do not accept that this makes the omission cost-free, but it is a defensible line, and it is better stated openly than sidestepped.

responses.point: El Manira says that if the citation is framed around therapy, Knudsen's claim is at least as strong as Mojsov's, and that framing around physiology is a judgement the committee should make openly rather than by default.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my configuration and I take it seriously. I think it is correct as a conditional: if the committee decided that the therapy is the achievement, my trio would be wrong and Knudsen would have to replace Mojsov or Drucker. I do not make that reading, because the physiology and the active peptide are what established the target and the sufficiency of the signal, and the analogue design is a considerable engineering step on that foundation. I also accept your caution on optogenetics. Your disclosure that B043 is close to your own field is helpful, and I would add that your attribution concern (Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck outside the trio) is the same one I have, so it is not an artefact of your proximity to the field. It is the reason B043 stays behind B003 and below B018 for me.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks the committee to settle the tool-versus-discovery principle before ranking optogenetics above CAR-T, argues that the Bamberg question is part of that choice, and proposes B018 as June and Sadelain only, with Rosenberg as a forerunner.
responses.response: I accept your sequencing and I have changed my own ordering of the two alternatives: B018 now goes first and B043 second, because the clinical proof for engineered T cells is unambiguous, whereas B043 needs a principle settled first. On Rosenberg, my round-1 view of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg as a trio is weaker after your argument. His adoptive transfer and early gene-modified T-cell trials are part of the clinical proof, but a prize that credits the CAR construct and its costimulatory design is more cleanly stated with June and Sadelain. I would still not move B018 into a second part with B003, since a two-part prize would cut the GLP-1 trio, and Eshhar's absence is a problem trimming to two does not solve. I also agree with you on cGAS-STING. A discovery resting on mechanism alone is acceptable in principle, but it is less urgent than a therapy that is already changing outcomes, and I now would not put a third name (Ishikawa) on it without a clearer account of STING priority.

responses.point: Sandberg argues that a June and Sadelain pair makes Eshhar's absence more conspicuous because it presents the engineering as the discovery, and that this is why B018 is an alternative and not a co-prize with B003.
responses.response: I think that is a fair point and it makes my own preference for a smaller B018 less clean. A pair implies that the credit is complete, and a trio including Rosenberg at least signals that the committee is crediting the clinical proof broadly. I do not see either fixing the Eshhar gap, and I do not think the committee should pretend otherwise. We agree that this makes B018 a standing alternative and not a second prize part this year. On your reading that the optogenetics tool-versus-discovery question can be answered, because the record includes methods that opened fields, I agree in principle, and the remaining problem is who the three are, not whether a method can qualify.

responses.point: The chair argues that the indirect medical impact of the unfolded protein response (B045) is a weaker objection than it first appears because proteostasis underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer, and he keeps Mori and Walter as a named alternative.
responses.response: I accept that the relevance to proteostasis in diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer is real and that I stated the objection too strongly in round 1. Mori and Walter is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and thirty years of confirmation counts for a lot. I still keep it outside my two alternatives, because those are the ones I would be ready to defend as a prize this year, and the link from the pathway to an approved therapy is not yet there, while B018 has an unambiguous clinical consequence and B043 an exceptional methodological one. If the committee prefers a pure mechanism prize, B045 is where I would look first, which is a different statement from ranking it high. On the chair's question about a mechanism-only prize, I find it acceptable in principle but not ahead of a therapy-backed discovery whose attribution we can defend.

uncertainties: Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide relative to Habener and other early investigators remains unresolved from the supplied material. I rely on recalled knowledge, have not verified it, and would want any committee record to say how it handled this question.
Whether the committee will frame the achievement around physiology (my trio) or around the therapy (which would put Knudsen against Mojsov). My configuration depends on the first reading.
Whether a trio from the six optogenetics names can be defended without a visible injustice, and whether the tool-versus-discovery principle should be settled first.
Whether B018 can be configured fairly without Eshhar, whether it should be June and Sadelain or include Rosenberg, and how Eshhar's absence should be handled.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My profile documents nuclear-receptor and dopamine-neuron research and past co-authorship with Ronald Evans (Salk), Johan Ericson, and fellow members Per Svenningsson (about twenty co-authored works, dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy) and Abdel El Manira (one paper, 2009). Round 1 shows that Svenningsson and El Manira have disclosed the same ties. None of these people or topics is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot, including the three names in my preferred B003 configuration and the alternatives B018 and B043. I do not infer ties from shared institutions or topics, and no recusal is needed.
